etymologyHint: A tall 高 mountain 山

components.note: Mountain — gives the base meaning of a peak or range.
Means 'tall/high' and reinforces that 嵩 describes a lofty, towering mountain.

example.hanzi: 嵩山是中国五岳之一。
example.pinyin: Sōngshān shì Zhōngguó wǔyuè zhī yī.
example.english: Mount Song is one of China's Five Great Mountains.
example.fact: The Five Great Mountains (五岳) are a set of five mountains in China that have been sites of imperial pilgrimage and worship for over two thousand years; Mount Song, in Henan, is the 'Central Mountain' and home to the Shaolin Temple.

meanings: to rinse one's mouth with water
etymologyHint: To gargle 欶 water 氵; 欶 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: The water radical, since gargling and rinsing involve water.
Read historically close to 'shuò' — close to, but not identical to, the modern reading 'shù'.

example.hanzi: 他每天早上漱口。
example.pinyin: Tā měitiān zǎoshang shùkǒu.
example.english: He rinses his mouth every morning.
example.fact: The compound 漱口 (to rinse one's mouth) is one of the oldest recorded hygiene habits in China — descriptions of mouth-rinsing after meals appear in texts from the Zhou dynasty, over 2,500 years ago.

components.note: Originally a pictograph of a wine jar; 酋 first meant 'mature, aged wine,' and the sense of 'chief' or 'elder leader' developed from the idea of something matured and respected.

example.hanzi: 部落的酋长决定了迁徙的时间。
example.pinyin: Bùluò de qiúzhǎng juédìngle qiānxǐ de shíjiān.
example.english: The tribal chief decided the time for migration.
example.fact: 酋长 (tribal chief) is the standard Chinese term used in anthropology and history texts to describe leaders of small-scale, kin-based societies around the world, from Native American tribes to Pacific Island communities.

components.note: 扌 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the hand.
襄 (xiāng) only loosely echoes "rǎng" — shares the "-ang" rime family but the initial and tone differ; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 他攘起袖子准备干活。
example.pinyin: Tā rǎngqǐ xiùzi zhǔnbèi gànhuó.
example.english: He pushed up his sleeves, ready to get to work.
example.fact: 攘 appears in the classical phrase 攘外安内 ('repel外部威胁, stabilize the interior'), a policy phrase describing how to handle both foreign threats and domestic unrest — quoted often in Chinese political history.

meanings: (bound form) to question closely; to interrogate

components.note: 讠 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to speech, words.
吉 (jí) is read identically to this character, "jí" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 老师诘问他为什么迟到。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī jíwèn tā wèishéme chídào.
example.english: The teacher questioned him closely about why he was late.
example.fact: 诘 is built from the speech radical 讠 plus 吉 ('lucky'), one of many characters where a component chosen purely for its sound (吉, 'jí') happens to carry an unrelated, auspicious meaning of its own.

components.note: 厶 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to something private or secret.
算 (suàn) shares its rime/vowel with "cuàn", both 4th tone, differing only in the initial consonant — a reasonably close, though not exact, match.

example.hanzi: 大臣篡夺了王位。
example.pinyin: Dàchén cuànduóle wángwèi.
example.english: The minister usurped the throne.
example.fact: 篡位 (usurping the throne) is a recurring theme in Chinese dynastic history — the Han dynasty was briefly interrupted when the official Wang Mang seized the throne in 9 CE, founding the short-lived Xin dynasty before the Han was restored.

components.note: The eye radical at the base suggests perception and insight, tying into the meaning 'astute, perceptive.'

example.hanzi: 这位领导以睿智著称。
example.pinyin: Zhè wèi lǐngdǎo yǐ ruìzhì zhùchēng.
example.english: This leader is renowned for his wisdom.
example.fact: 睿 is a common character in Chinese emperors' posthumous or temple names — for example, several Tang and Qing rulers carried titles including 睿, meaning 'wise and perceptive,' as a mark of praise for good governance.

etymologyHint: A jade statue 王 with four holes made in it 口

components.note: The repeated 口 (mouth) shapes are thought to represent cries of alarm or distress, tying into the character's meaning of 'shocking, ill-omened.'

example.hanzi: 这真是一场噩梦。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhēnshi yī chǎng èmèng.
example.english: This is truly a nightmare.
example.fact: 噩耗 ('shocking news,' almost always meaning news of a death) and 噩梦 ('nightmare') are the two most common words built from 噩 — the character rarely appears outside contexts of bad news or dread.

components.note: 忄 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the heart, emotion.
长 (cháng) shares the same base sound as "chàng", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 听到这个消息，她感到很怅然。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège xiāoxi, tā gǎndào hěn chàngrán.
example.english: Hearing this news, she felt disappointed and dejected.
example.fact: 怅 combines the heart radical 忄 with 长 (cháng, 'long'), a common pairing in emotion characters where 忄 marks the meaning and the right-hand part supplies a sound that, here, isn't especially close to the modern reading 'chàng.'

components.note: 皿 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a dish or vessel.
央 (yāng) shares its rime/vowel with "àng", though the tone and the missing initial "y-" set them apart — a reasonably close, though not exact, match.

example.hanzi: 屋子里洋溢着盎然的生机。
example.pinyin: Wūzi lǐ yángyìzhe àngrán de shēngjī.
example.english: The room was brimming with vibrant life.
example.fact: 盎 originally described a large-bellied pottery jar; the sense of 'brimming, abundant' in words like 盎然 (as in 春意盎然, 'spring is in full bloom') comes directly from the image of a jar filled to overflowing.

etymologyHint: To step 彳 out on a long journey 歨

components.note: This 'walking' radical marks the character as related to movement — appropriate for a word meaning 'to relocate, migrate.'

example.hanzi: 候鸟每年都会迁徙。
example.pinyin: Hòuniǎo měinián dōu huì qiānxǐ.
example.english: Migratory birds relocate every year.
example.fact: Some migratory birds, like the Arctic tern, travel over 70,000 kilometers round-trip each year between the Arctic and Antarctic — one of the longest migrations of any animal on Earth.

meanings: wooden yoke for a draft ox

components.note: 革 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to leather, hide.
央 (yāng) is read identically to this character, "yāng" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 马鞅套在马的脖子上。
example.pinyin: Mǎyāng tào zài mǎ de bózi shàng.
example.english: The martingale strap is fitted around the horse's neck.
example.fact: 鞅 is built from the leather radical 革, reflecting that harness parts in ancient China — like the yoke strap it names — were traditionally made from tanned animal hide.

components.note: 氵 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to water.
离 (lí) is read identically to this character, "lí" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 漓江的风景非常美丽。
example.pinyin: Líjiāng de fēngjǐng fēicháng měilì.
example.english: The scenery of the Li River is extremely beautiful.
example.fact: The Li River in Guangxi, referenced in this character's meaning, flows past the karst peaks of Guilin and Yangshuo — a landscape so distinctive it is depicted on the back of the 20-yuan Chinese banknote.

components.note: 示 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a spirit, the supernatural.

example.hanzi: 他做事总是鬼鬼祟祟的。
example.pinyin: Tā zuòshì zǒngshì guǐguǐsuìsuì de.
example.english: He always acts in a sneaky, suspicious way.
example.fact: 祟 is built from 示 (an altar or spirit-related radical) and 出 ('to emerge'), reflecting the old belief that misfortune or illness could 'emerge' from an evil spirit's influence — the character's original meaning.

components.note: 目 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the eye.
疌 (jié) is read identically to this character, "jié" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 她的睫毛又长又密。
example.pinyin: Tā de jiémáo yòu cháng yòu mì.
example.english: Her eyelashes are long and thick.
example.fact: Human eyelashes typically last only about 3 months before falling out and being replaced, one of the fastest hair-growth cycles on the human body.

components.note: The person radical suggests a person walking or proceeding — related to the sense of something 'flowing along' or being 'distant.'
A 'strike/act' radical often seen in characters about ongoing action; here it reinforces the sense of continuing motion in 攸's original meaning.

example.hanzi: 这件事关系攸关，不能马虎。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì guānxì yōuguān, bùnéng mǎhu.
example.english: This matter is of vital importance and cannot be handled carelessly.
example.fact: 攸 survives in modern Mandarin almost entirely inside the fixed phrase 攸关 ('to have a vital bearing on'), as in 生死攸关 ('a matter of life and death') — a rare case of an ancient character kept alive by a single compound.

components.note: 羽 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to feathers, plumage.
令 (lìng) shares the same base sound as "líng", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 孔雀的翎毛五彩斑斓。
example.pinyin: Kǒngquè de língmáo wǔcǎi bānlán.
example.english: The peacock's plumage is brilliantly colorful.
example.fact: Peacock tail feathers get their iridescent color not from pigment but from microscopic structures that bend light — the same physical principle, called structural coloration, that makes soap bubbles shimmer.

meanings: to choke (because of swallowing the wrong way)

components.note: 口 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the mouth.
仓 (cāng) only loosely echoes "qiāng" — sharing only the "-ang" rime; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 浓烟让他呛得直咳嗽。
example.pinyin: Nóngyān ràng tā qiàng de zhí késòu.
example.english: The thick smoke made him choke and cough repeatedly.
example.fact: Choking on smoke, as this sentence describes, is what makes house fires so dangerous — most fire deaths are caused by smoke inhalation rather than by burns.

components.note: ⺮ is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to bamboo.
匡 (kuāng) is read identically to this character, "kuāng" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 篮子里装着一筐苹果。
example.pinyin: Lánzi lǐ zhuāngzhe yī kuāng píngguǒ.
example.english: The basket holds a hamper of apples.
example.fact: 筐 is written with the bamboo radical 竹 because woven bamboo baskets have been a standard household container in China for thousands of years, long before plastic or metal alternatives existed.

components.note: 土 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to earth, soil.
斩 (zhǎn) no longer sounds close to "qiàn" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 护城河是一道深深的堑壕。
example.pinyin: Hùchénghé shì yī dào shēnshēn de qiànháo.
example.english: The moat is a deep trench.
example.fact: Moats surrounding medieval castles and Chinese city walls served a dual purpose: they slowed attackers and, because most were connected to rivers, doubled as a water supply during a siege.

components.note: 木 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to wood, a tree.
亶 (dǎn)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "tán" (both are alveolar stop consonants), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 檀香的味道让人放松。
example.pinyin: Tánxiāng de wèidào ràng rén fàngsōng.
example.english: The scent of sandalwood is relaxing.
example.fact: Sandalwood is one of the most expensive woods in the world by weight, prized for millennia in perfume, incense, and traditional medicine across India, China, and the Middle East.

components.note: The roof/house radical at the top; in this character it is thought to relate to the idea of respectful conduct within the home, tied to 寅's older meaning 'to respect.'

example.hanzi: 寅时是凌晨三点到五点。
example.pinyin: Yínshí shì língchén sān diǎn dào wǔ diǎn.
example.english: The 'yin' hour is from 3 to 5 a.m.
example.fact: 寅 is the third of the twelve Earthly Branches used in the traditional Chinese calendar; it corresponds to the Year of the Tiger and to the two-hour period from 3 a.m. to 5 a.m. in the old system of dividing the day.

components.note: Three copies of 'stone' (石) stacked together directly picture a pile of rocks — the character's core meaning.

example.hanzi: 他为人光明磊落。
example.pinyin: Tā wéirén guāngmíng lěiluò.
example.english: He is an open and honest person.
example.fact: 磊 is one of a small set of Chinese characters formed by simply tripling a single component — 森 (forest, from three 木) and 淼 (vast waters, from three 水) follow the same visual logic of 'three of a thing means a lot of it.'

components.note: 马 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a horse.
又 (yòu) only loosely echoes "yù" — sharing only the initial "y-"; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 骑手熟练地驭马前行。
example.pinyin: Qíshǒu shúliàn de yùmǎ qiánxíng.
example.english: The rider skillfully controlled the horse forward.
example.fact: 驭 appears in 驾驭 ('to control, to master'), a word now used far more often in the abstract sense of mastering a skill or situation than in its literal meaning of driving a horse-drawn vehicle.

components.note: 忄 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the heart, emotion.
罔 (wǎng) is read identically to this character, "wǎng" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 面对未来，他感到一片迷惘。
example.pinyin: Miànduì wèilái, tā gǎndào yī piàn míwǎng.
example.english: Facing the future, he felt completely lost.
example.fact: 惘 always appears with the heart radical 忄 because in traditional Chinese thought, the 心 (heart) — not the brain — was considered the seat of thought, confusion, and emotion.

etymologyHint: The sound a dog 犬 makes with their mouth 口

components.note: Mouth — the sound-making body part, since barking comes from the mouth.
Dog — identifies whose sound is being described.

example.hanzi: 邻居家的狗整夜狂吠。
example.pinyin: Línjū jiā de gǒu zhěngyè kuángfèi.
example.english: The neighbor's dog barked wildly all night.
example.fact: The idiom 鸡鸣狗吠 ('roosters crowing, dogs barking') is used in Chinese to evoke the ordinary sounds of a peaceful, everyday village — a rural counterpart to the English phrase 'the hustle and bustle of daily life.'

meanings: load carried by a pack animal

components.note: 马 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a horse.
大 (dà) no longer sounds close to "tuó" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 骆驼驮着沉重的货物。
example.pinyin: Luòtuo tuózhe chénzhòng de huòwù.
example.english: The camel carries heavy goods on its back.
example.fact: A camel can carry loads of over 150 kilograms across deserts for days at a time, which is exactly why camel caravans became the backbone of the ancient Silk Road trade routes.

meanings: used in 瑪瑙|玛瑙[ma3 nao3]

components.note: 王 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to jade.

example.hanzi: 她戴着一条玛瑙项链。
example.pinyin: Tā dàizhe yī tiáo mǎnǎo xiàngliàn.
example.english: She is wearing an agate necklace.
example.fact: Agate forms inside volcanic rock cavities as silica-rich water deposits mineral layers over thousands of years, which is why a single polished agate slice often shows dozens of distinct concentric bands.

components.note: 火 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to fire.
巨 (jù) is read identically to this character, "jù" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 运动员举着火炬跑进体育场。
example.pinyin: Yùndòngyuán jǔzhe huǒjù pǎojìn tǐyùchǎng.
example.english: The athlete ran into the stadium holding the torch.
example.fact: The Olympic torch relay was not part of the ancient Games — it was introduced at the 1936 Berlin Olympics and has been a tradition at every Games since.

components.note: 疒 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to sickness, illness.

example.hanzi: 高烧引发了孩子的痉挛。
example.pinyin: Gāoshāo yǐnfāle háizi de jìngluán.
example.english: The high fever triggered a convulsion in the child.
example.fact: Febrile convulsions (fever-triggered seizures), like the one in this sentence, affect roughly 2-5% of children under age five and are usually harmless, even though they look alarming.

meanings: expose or dry in the sun

components.note: 日 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the sun.
暴's everyday reading is "bào" (as in 曝光, "to expose"), which matches this character's alternate reading exactly; the "pù" reading used here is a more literary variant.

example.hanzi: 这条新闻已经在网上曝光了。
example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo xīnwén yǐjīng zài wǎngshàng bàoguāngle.
example.english: This piece of news has already been exposed online.
example.fact: The word 曝光 ('to expose,' now meaning to expose wrongdoing publicly) comes directly from photography — it originally described exposing a light-sensitive photographic plate or film to light.

components.note: 忄 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the heart, emotion.
岂 (qǐ) no longer sounds close to "kǎi" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 恺字常用于人名，寓意快乐。
example.pinyin: Kǎi zì chángyòng yú rénmíng, yùyì kuàilè.
example.english: The character 恺 is often used in people's names, symbolizing joy.
example.fact: 恺 shares its right-hand component 岂 with the character 凯 (triumphant victory) — both carry connotations of joy and triumph, which is why they are common choices in given names.

components.note: ⺼ is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to flesh, the body.
安 (ān) shares the same base sound as "àn", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 胺是一类含氮的有机化合物。
example.pinyin: Àn shì yī lèi hán dàn de yǒujī huàhéwù.
example.english: Amines are a class of organic compounds containing nitrogen.
example.fact: Amines are essential to life — the amino acids that build every protein in your body are named for the amine group (-NH2) chemically attached to them.

components.note: 虫 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to an insect or small creature.

example.hanzi: 夏夜里飞舞着许多萤火虫。
example.pinyin: Xiàyè lǐ fēiwǔzhe xǔduō yínghuǒchóng.
example.english: Many fireflies fly about on summer nights.
example.fact: Fireflies produce light through a chemical reaction called bioluminescence, and their flashing patterns are actually species-specific signals used to find and attract mates in the dark.

components.note: 攵 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to an action, a striking motion.
束 (shù) no longer sounds close to "chì" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 皇帝颁布了一道敕令。
example.pinyin: Huángdì bānbùle yī dào chìlìng.
example.english: The emperor issued an imperial edict.
example.fact: 敕 was reserved specifically for orders issued by an emperor — using the word to describe an ordinary person's command would have been a serious breach of etiquette in imperial China.

components.note: ⺮ is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to bamboo.
争 (zhēng) is read identically to this character, "zhēng" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 他弹奏了一首古筝曲子。
example.pinyin: Tā tánzòule yī shǒu gǔzhēng qǔzi.
example.english: He played a piece of music on the guzheng.
example.fact: The guzheng (古筝), the plucked string instrument named with this character, has a documented history of over 2,500 years, making it one of the oldest musical instruments still played in China today.

components.note: 巾 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to cloth.
番 (fān) is read identically to this character, "fān" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 寺庙前挂着一面幡。
example.pinyin: Sìmiào qián guàzhe yī miàn fān.
example.english: A banner hangs in front of the temple.
example.fact: Long vertical banners like the 幡 in this sentence are traditionally hung at Buddhist temples in China, often inscribed with sutras or prayers, and are believed to generate merit for those who view them fluttering in the wind.

meanings: used in 霹靂|霹雳[pi1 li4] and 霹雷[pi1 lei2]

components.note: 雨 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to rain.
辟 (pì) shares the same base sound as "pī", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 一声霹雳划破了夜空。
example.pinyin: Yī shēng pīlì huàpòle yèkōng.
example.english: A crash of thunder split the night sky.
example.fact: Thunder is the sound created by the rapid expansion of air superheated by a lightning bolt to roughly 30,000 Kelvin — hotter than the surface of the sun — in a fraction of a second.

etymologyHint: A kind 二 of bamboo ⺮; ⺮ also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Bamboo radical, the character's original literal meaning before it came to also denote ancient India (天竺).

example.hanzi: 天竺是古代中国对印度的称呼。
example.pinyin: Tiānzhú shì gǔdài Zhōngguó duì Yìndù de chēnghū.
example.english: 'Tianzhu' was the ancient Chinese name for India.
example.fact: The name 天竺 for India was used by the famous monk Xuanzang, whose 7th-century pilgrimage along the Silk Road to study Buddhism in India later inspired the classic novel 'Journey to the West.'

components.note: 火 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to fire.
各 (gè) no longer sounds close to "lào" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 铁匠用烙铁在木头上留下印记。
example.pinyin: Tiějiang yòng làotiě zài mùtou shàng liúxià yìnjì.
example.english: The blacksmith used a branding iron to leave a mark on the wood.
example.fact: The word 烙印 ('brand mark') is used figuratively in Chinese much like 'branded' or 'scarred' in English, to describe an experience that leaves a permanent psychological mark.

components.note: 田 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a field.
比 (bǐ)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "pí" (b- and p- are closely related bilabial sounds), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 两个村子毗邻而建。
example.pinyin: Liǎng gè cūnzi pílín ér jiàn.
example.english: The two villages were built adjoining each other.
example.fact: 毗 survives in modern Chinese almost exclusively in the compound 毗邻 ('adjacent to, bordering'), commonly used in geography and legal documents to describe neighboring regions or properties.

components.note: 鸟 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a bird.
九 (jiǔ) shares the same base sound as "jiū", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 鸠是一种常见的鸟类。
example.pinyin: Jiū shì yī zhǒng chángjiàn de niǎolèi.
example.english: The turtledove is a common type of bird.
example.fact: The turtledove (鸠) appears in one of the oldest poems in the Chinese literary canon, the 'Book of Songs' (诗经), compiled around 3,000 years ago, where birds are frequently used as symbols in romantic verse.

components.note: 土 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to earth, soil.
阜 (fù)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "bù" (Mandarin "f-" often historically derives from an older "b-"/"p-" sound), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 上海曾是一个繁忙的商埠。
example.pinyin: Shànghǎi céng shì yī gè fánmáng de shāngbù.
example.english: Shanghai was once a bustling trading port.
example.fact: After the 1842 Treaty of Nanking, Shanghai became one of China's first 'treaty ports' (商埠) opened to foreign trade — a status that transformed it within decades into one of Asia's largest commercial cities.

components.note: 艹 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a plant, grass.
祘 (suàn) is read identically to this character, "suàn" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 妈妈在炒菜时加了一些蒜。
example.pinyin: Māma zài chǎocài shí jiāle yīxiē suàn.
example.english: Mom added some garlic while stir-frying.
example.fact: Garlic's pungent smell comes from allicin, a sulfur compound that only forms when the plant's cells are damaged by cutting or crushing — an evolved chemical defense against pests.

components.note: The left-side form of this character (used as a radical in other characters) originally pictured a stepped hill or mound, matching 阜's core meaning of 'mound.'

example.hanzi: 物产丰阜是这个地区的特点。
example.pinyin: Wùchǎn fēngfù shì zhège dìqū de tèdiǎn.
example.english: Abundant produce is a feature of this region.
example.fact: 阜 is the origin of the 'left-ear' radical 阝 (阜旁) that appears in many characters related to hills, mounds, and terrain, such as 陡 (steep) and 阻 (obstruct).

components.note: 口 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the mouth.
曹 (cáo) is read identically to this character, "cáo" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 市场里人声嘈杂。
example.pinyin: Shìchǎng lǐ rénshēng cáozá.
example.english: The market was noisy with the sound of people's voices.
example.fact: 嘈杂 (noisy, clamorous) is one of many Chinese onomatopoeic-flavored words built with the mouth radical 口, a visual cue that groups characters describing sounds people make.

meanings: used with pong for ping pong
etymologyHint: A ball bouncing back and forth; compare 乓

components.note: Visually resembles a small mound or bounce; combined with 乓, the pair of characters were coined together to imitate the back-and-forth sound of a ball bouncing.

example.hanzi: 我们周末喜欢打乒乓球。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zhōumò xǐhuan dǎ pīngpāngqiú.
example.english: We like to play ping pong on weekends.
example.fact: 乒 and 乓 are onomatopoeic characters coined together purely for the sound of a table tennis ball bouncing — table tennis itself is sometimes called China's 'national game,' and Chinese teams have dominated Olympic table tennis since it became an Olympic sport in 1988.

components.note: 巾 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to cloth.
隹 (zhuī) no longer sounds close to "wéi" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 舞台后面挂着厚厚的帷幕。
example.pinyin: Wǔtái hòumiàn guàzhe hòuhòu de wéimù.
example.english: A thick curtain hangs behind the stage.
example.fact: 帷幕 (stage curtain) gives rise to the common idiom 拉开帷幕 ('to raise the curtain'), used figuratively in Chinese news writing to mean 'to kick off' any major event, much like the English phrase.

components.note: 口 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the mouth.

豖 (chù)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "zhuó" (ch- and zh- are closely related retroflex sounds, and the rimes are similar), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 啄木鸟在树上啄食虫子。
example.pinyin: Zhuómùniǎo zài shù shàng zhuóshí chóngzi.
example.english: The woodpecker pecks at insects on the tree.
example.fact: A woodpecker can strike a tree up to 20 times per second, and its skull has a spongy, shock-absorbing bone structure that keeps its brain safe from the repeated impact.

components.note: 鱼 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a fish.
敖 (áo) is read identically to this character, "áo" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 传说中鳌驮着一座仙山。
example.pinyin: Chuánshuō zhōng áo tuózhe yī zuò xiānshān.
example.english: In legend, the giant sea turtle carries a mythical mountain on its back.
example.fact: In Chinese mythology, giant sea turtles called 鳌 were said to support the mythical islands where immortals lived — a similar 'world-turtle' motif appears independently in Hindu and some Native American mythologies.

components.note: 毛 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to fur, hair.
占 (zhàn) shares the same base sound as "zhān", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 冬天他喜欢盖毡子。
example.pinyin: Dōngtiān tā xǐhuan gài zhānzi.
example.english: In winter he likes to cover himself with a felt blanket.
example.fact: Felt, made by matting and pressing fibers together rather than weaving them, is believed to be one of the oldest textiles in human history, with felt artifacts found in Central Asian nomadic tombs dating back over 2,500 years.

components.note: 门 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a gate or door.
欮 (jué)'s own standalone reading is obscure today, so its exact historical closeness to "quē" is hard to verify with confidence.

example.hanzi: 古代宫殿前常有壮观的阙楼。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài gōngdiàn qián cháng yǒu zhuàngguān de quèlóu.
example.english: Ancient palaces often had magnificent watchtowers in front.
example.fact: 阙 gave its name to Tiananmen (天安门), whose full formal architecture in imperial times included flanking watchtower structures descended from the ancient 阙 gate-towers that marked the entrance to a palace complex.

components.note: 衤 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to clothing.
辱 (rù) is read identically to this character, "rù" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 床上铺着厚厚的褥子。
example.pinyin: Chuáng shàng pūzhe hòuhòu de rùzi.
example.english: A thick mattress pad is spread on the bed.
example.fact: 褥 is written with the clothing radical 衤 because in traditional Chinese homes, a 褥子 was a padded cotton or wool mat rather than a Western-style sprung mattress.

etymologyHint: To scratch 扌 a flea bite 蚤; 蚤 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Hand radical — scratching is done with the hand.
Means 'flea'; historically it lends a reading close to but not identical to modern 'sāo' — chosen partly because flea bites are a classic reason to scratch.

example.hanzi: 蚊子咬得他直搔痒。
example.pinyin: Wénzi yǎo de tā zhí sāoyǎng.
example.english: The mosquito bites made him scratch himself constantly.
example.fact: Scratching an itch temporarily relieves it because the mild pain it creates causes the brain to release serotonin, which can, ironically, make the itch return more intensely a short while later.

components.note: ⺮ is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to bamboo.
尹 (yǐn) no longer sounds close to "sǔn" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 春天是挖竹笋的好时节。
example.pinyin: Chūntiān shì wā zhúsǔn de hǎo shíjié.
example.english: Spring is a good season for digging up bamboo shoots.
example.fact: Bamboo shoots are among the fastest-growing plant structures on Earth — some species can grow over 90 centimeters in a single day, visibly lengthening within hours.

components.note: 冂 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to an enclosure or covering.
免 (miǎn) is read identically to this character, "miǎn" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 国王头戴金色的皇冕。
example.pinyin: Guówáng tóudài jīnsè de huángmiǎn.
example.english: The king wore a golden crown on his head.
example.fact: The character 冕 specifically named the flat-topped ceremonial crown worn by Chinese emperors and high officials, which hung strings of jade beads in front of the eyes to remind the wearer not to look at trivial things.

components.note: 犭 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a dog or four-legged animal.
宁 (níng) is read identically to this character, "níng" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 他狰狞的表情吓到了孩子。
example.pinyin: Tā zhēngníng de biǎoqíng xiàdàole háizi.
example.english: His ferocious expression frightened the child.
example.fact: 狞 almost always appears paired with 狰 in the compound 狰狞 ('fierce-looking, hideous') — like many two-character words in Chinese, neither character alone carries the full meaning as commonly in modern speech.

etymologyHint: Imperial 召 music 音; 召 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Sound/music radical — 韶 originally named a legendary style of ceremonial music attributed to the sage-king Shun.
Gives a reading close to but not identical to 'sháo'.

example.hanzi: 他常常怀念自己的韶华岁月。
example.pinyin: Tā chángcháng huáiniàn zìjǐ de sháohuá suìyuè.
example.english: He often reminisces about his youthful years.
example.fact: 韶 survives today mainly in the poetic phrase 韶华 ('the prime of one's youth'), tracing back to the legendary emperor Shun, whose court music, called 韶乐, Confucius himself praised as the height of musical perfection.

components.note: 骨 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to bone.
各 (gè) shares the same base sound as "gé", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 医生检查了他的骨骼。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng jiǎnchále tā de gǔgé.
example.english: The doctor examined his skeleton.
example.fact: The adult human skeleton contains 206 bones, down from about 300 at birth — many bones fuse together naturally as a child grows into adulthood.

components.note: 艹 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a plant, grass.
谒 (yè) no longer sounds close to "ǎi" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 老师对学生总是和蔼可亲。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī duì xuéshēng zǒngshì hé'ǎi kěqīn.
example.english: The teacher is always warm and friendly to the students.
example.fact: 和蔼 (kind, affable) pairs 蔼 with 和 ('harmonious'), reflecting how Chinese frequently builds descriptions of personality by combining two near-synonymous characters for emphasis.

components.note: 灬 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to fire.
亨 (hēng) only loosely echoes "pēng" — sharing only the "-eng" rime; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 妈妈在厨房里烹饪晚饭。
example.pinyin: Māma zài chúfáng lǐ pēngrèn wǎnfàn.
example.english: Mom is cooking dinner in the kitchen.
example.fact: The word 烹饪 (cooking, cuisine) combines 烹 ('to boil/cook') and 饪 ('to cook until done') — together they form the standard formal term for 'cuisine' used in Chinese culinary and academic contexts.

components.note: 'Big' — in this character it contributes to an old sense of covering or overspreading something broadly.

example.hanzi: 病人已经奄奄一息了。
example.pinyin: Bìngrén yǐjīng yǎnyǎn yī xī le.
example.english: The patient is already at their last gasp.
example.fact: 奄 survives in modern Mandarin almost entirely through the phrase 奄奄一息 ('breathing one's last, at the point of death'), a vivid example of how many ancient characters are kept alive today only inside a single fixed idiom.

components.note: 女 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a woman.
票 (piào) shares the same base sound as "piáo", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 小说里描写了一个嫖客的堕落。
example.pinyin: Xiǎoshuō lǐ miáoxiěle yī gè piáokè de duòluò.
example.english: The novel depicts the moral decline of a man who visits prostitutes.
example.fact: 嫖 is written with the woman radical 女, one of many characters in Chinese related to women or gender roles that historically carried this radical, reflecting old-fashioned and often biased conventions embedded in the writing system itself.

components.note: 氵 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to water.
木 (mù) is read identically to this character, "mù" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 他每天早上都会沐浴。
example.pinyin: Tā měitiān zǎoshang dōu huì mùyù.
example.english: He bathes every morning.
example.fact: 沐浴 traditionally distinguished two parts of washing: 沐 specifically meant washing the hair, while 浴 meant washing the body — a distinction still visible in the character's radical, 木 ('tree/wood'), hinting at washing with water poured from above like rain through leaves.

components.note: 口 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the mouth.
菐 (pú) shares the same base sound as "pū", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 气球突然噗地一声破了。
example.pinyin: Qìqiú tūrán pū de yī shēng pòle.
example.english: The balloon suddenly burst with a pop.
example.fact: 噗 is a purely onomatopoeic character, built from the mouth radical 口, used across Chinese to represent soft bursting, popping, or puffing sounds — similar to how English uses 'pop' or 'puff.'

components.note: 山 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a mountain.
今 (jīn) no longer sounds close to "cén" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 岑姓在中国并不多见。
example.pinyin: Cén xìng zài Zhōngguó bìng bù duōjiàn.
example.english: The surname Cen is not very common in China.
example.fact: 岑 today functions mainly as a surname and in place names describing small, steep hills — its everyday meaning of 'peak' has largely been replaced by more common characters like 峰 in modern speech.

meanings: see also 蛟龍|蛟龙[jiao1 long2]

components.note: 虫 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to an insect or small creature.
交 (jiāo) is read identically to this character, "jiāo" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 传说中的蛟龙能腾云驾雾。
example.pinyin: Chuánshuō zhōng de jiāolóng néng téngyún jiàwù.
example.english: The legendary scaly dragon can ride the clouds and mist.
example.fact: 蛟 describes a specific type of dragon in Chinese mythology, distinct from the more famous 龙 (long, the imperial dragon) — 蛟 was traditionally associated with rivers and floods rather than the sky.

etymologyHint: To catch 虏 someone by the hand 扌; 虏 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Hand radical — capturing someone by force involves the hands.
Means 'captive'; provides both the sound and a closely related meaning.

example.hanzi: 海盗掳走了村里的财物。
example.pinyin: Hǎidào lǔzǒule cūn lǐ de cáiwù.
example.english: The pirates seized the village's valuables.
example.fact: 掳掠 ('to plunder, to loot') pairs two nearly synonymous characters, 掳 and 掠, a common pattern in Chinese where two-character compound words reinforce meaning through near-repetition.

components.note: 口 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the mouth.
永 (yǒng) is read identically to this character, "yǒng" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 诗人咏叹着大自然的美丽。
example.pinyin: Shīrén yǒngtàn zhe dàzìrán de měilì.
example.english: The poet sings the praises of nature's beauty.
example.fact: 咏 gives its name to a whole genre of classical Chinese poetry called 咏物诗 ('poems chanting/praising an object'), in which poets used a single object — a plum blossom, a crane, the moon — as a vehicle for deeper reflection.

components.note: 弓 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a bow.
奴 (nú) shares the same base sound as "nǔ", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 古代士兵使用弩来射箭。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài shìbīng shǐyòng nǔ lái shèjiàn.
example.english: Ancient soldiers used crossbows to shoot arrows.
example.fact: The crossbow was a major Chinese military innovation of the Warring States period (5th–3rd century BCE) — its trigger mechanism let relatively untrained soldiers fire with power and accuracy that previously required years of archery training.

meanings: to twist or nip with the fingers

components.note: 扌 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the hand.
念 (niàn) shares the same base sound as "niǎn", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 她用手指捻着一根线。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng shǒuzhǐ niǎnzhe yī gēn xiàn.
example.english: She twirled a thread between her fingers.
example.fact: 捻 describes the same fine motor motion used in traditional hand-spinning of thread — a technique practiced for thousands of years before mechanical spinning wheels and industrial spinning machines were invented.

components.note: 囗 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to an enclosure, a boundary.
甫 (fǔ)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "pǔ" (f- historically derives from an older "b-"/"p-" sound), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 奶奶在后院种了一个菜圃。
example.pinyin: Nǎinai zài hòuyuàn zhòngle yī gè càipǔ.
example.english: Grandma planted a vegetable garden in the backyard.
example.fact: 圃 is enclosed by the 囗 radical, visually depicting a plot of land with a boundary — a fitting shape for a character meaning a cultivated garden or field.

etymologyHint: A bird clutching 爫 its eggs 子

components.note: A stylized hand or claw shape, here depicting a bird's claw grasping something, tying into the character's original image of a bird brooding over its eggs.
Means 'child/offspring' — represents the eggs being tended, the source of the extended meaning 'to trust, to have confidence in.'

example.hanzi: 他的努力深孚众望。
example.pinyin: Tā de nǔlì shēn fú zhòngwàng.
example.english: His efforts truly live up to everyone's expectations.
example.fact: 孚's original picture — a claw over a child/egg — reflects how the abstract meaning 'trustworthy, to inspire confidence' grew from the very concrete image of a bird patiently and reliably brooding over its eggs until they hatch.

components.note: 忄 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the heart, emotion.
卒 (zú) only loosely echoes "cuì" — the initials z-/c- are related, but the rimes differ; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 长期的压力让他面容憔悴。
example.pinyin: Chángqī de yālì ràng tā miànróng qiáocuì.
example.english: Long-term stress has left his face haggard.
example.fact: 憔悴 (haggard, careworn) is composed of two characters that individually mean almost the same thing, a very common structure in Chinese vocabulary that helps distinguish a word from a single homophone character.

meanings: one's current attainment in learning or art
etymologyHint: To meet 讠 a goal 旨; 旨 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Speech radical — 诣 originally meant 'to visit and pay respects to a superior,' an act typically involving formal speech.
Means 'purpose, aim'; lends a reading close to, but not identical to, 'yì', and also echoes the sense of 'reaching a goal' in 诣's modern meaning of 'attainment.'

example.hanzi: 他在书法方面造诣很深。
example.pinyin: Tā zài shūfǎ fāngmiàn zàoyì hěn shēn.
example.english: He has deep attainment in the art of calligraphy.
example.fact: 造诣 ('level of attainment,' as in mastery of an art or field) is one of the most common academic and cultural compliments in Chinese, used to praise a lifetime of accumulated skill rather than a single achievement.

components.note: 口 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the mouth.
瓜 (guā) shares its rime/vowel with "gū" — a reasonably close, though not exact, match.

example.hanzi: 婴儿呱呱地哭了起来。
example.pinyin: Yīng'ér gūgū de kūle qǐlái.
example.english: The baby began crying with a waa-waa sound.
example.fact: 呱呱 is the standard Chinese onomatopoeia for a newborn's first cry, giving rise to the idiom 呱呱坠地 ('to fall to the ground crying'), a poetic way of saying 'to be born.'

components.note: 礻 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a spirit, the supernatural.
阝 here is a compressed form of 邑 ("settlement, place"); it doesn't have a clear standalone reading of its own, so its historical closeness to "qí" is hard to verify with confidence.

example.hanzi: 祁姓在山西一带较为常见。
example.pinyin: Qí xìng zài Shānxī yīdài jiào wéi chángjiàn.
example.english: The surname Qi is relatively common in the Shanxi region.
example.fact: 祁 today functions mainly as a surname and in place names, such as 祁门 in Anhui province, famous for producing Keemun black tea, one of China's most celebrated tea exports.

components.note: 扌 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the hand.
垂 (chuí) is read identically to this character, "chuí" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 他用拳头捶打着桌子。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng quántou chuídǎzhe zhuōzi.
example.english: He pounded the table with his fist.
example.fact: 捶 shares its right-hand phonetic component 垂 with 锤 ('hammer'), a related character describing the tool used for exactly this kind of pounding motion.

components.note: 钅 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to metal.
内 (nà) is read identically to this character, "nà" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 钠是人体不可缺少的元素。
example.pinyin: Nà shì réntǐ bùkě quēshǎo de yuánsù.
example.english: Sodium is an essential element for the human body.
example.fact: Sodium is so chemically reactive that pure metallic sodium bursts into flame or explodes on contact with water — yet combined with chlorine as table salt, it becomes a stable, essential part of the human diet.

meanings: short and lined coat or robe

components.note: 衤 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to clothing.
夭 (yāo) shares its rime/vowel with "ǎo" — a reasonably close, though not exact, match.

example.hanzi: 冬天她穿上了厚厚的棉袄。
example.pinyin: Dōngtiān tā chuānshàngle hòuhòu de mián'ǎo.
example.english: In winter she put on a thick padded cotton jacket.
example.fact: 棉袄 (padded cotton jacket) was the standard winter garment across northern China for centuries before down jackets and synthetic insulation became widely available in the late 20th century.

components.note: 氵 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to water.
彭 (péng) shares the same base sound as "pēng", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 海浪澎湃地拍打着岸边。
example.pinyin: Hǎilàng péngpài de pāidǎzhe ànbiān.
example.english: The waves crashed powerfully against the shore.
example.fact: 澎湃 (surging, crashing) is almost always used together as a pair — like many two-character Chinese words describing sound or motion, splitting the pair apart removes most of its vivid, dynamic feel.

components.note: 气 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to gas, vapor.
炎 (yán) no longer sounds close to "dàn" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 空气中氮气占了大约百分之七十八。
example.pinyin: Kōngqì zhōng dànqì zhànle dàyuē bǎifēnzhī qīshíbā.
example.english: Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of the air.
example.fact: Nitrogen gas makes up roughly 78% of Earth's atmosphere, far more than oxygen's 21% — yet most living things cannot use atmospheric nitrogen directly and rely on specialized bacteria to convert it into usable forms.

components.note: 忄 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the heart, emotion.
各 (gè)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "kè" (g- and k- are closely related velar sounds, and the rime and tone match), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 他一直恪守着自己的原则。
example.pinyin: Tā yīzhí kèshǒuzhe zìjǐ de yuánzé.
example.english: He has always strictly adhered to his own principles.
example.fact: 恪守 ('to strictly abide by') is frequently used in formal Chinese writing about ethics, law, and diplomacy — its tone is notably more solemn and formal than the everyday word 遵守 ('to comply with').

components.note: 隹 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a short-tailed bird.
刍 (chú) is read identically to this character, "chú" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 母鸡带着一群雏鸟散步。
example.pinyin: Mǔjī dàizhe yī qún chúniǎo sànbù.
example.english: The hen walks around with a group of chicks.
example.fact: 雏 gives its name to 雏鸟 (chick, fledgling) and is also used metaphorically in words like 雏形 ('the initial, rough shape of something'), applying the idea of an early, undeveloped stage to abstract plans and projects.

meanings: to pick up (a powder etc) with the fingertips

components.note: 扌 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the hand.
最 (zuì) only loosely echoes "cuō" — the initials z-/c- are related, but the rimes differ; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 厨师撮了一小撮盐放进锅里。
example.pinyin: Chúshī cuōle yī xiǎo cuō yán fàng jìn guō lǐ.
example.english: The chef pinched a small pinch of salt into the pot.
example.fact: 撮 is also the character used in 撮合 ('to bring two parties together, to matchmake'), extending the physical idea of gathering small things together with the fingers into the social idea of bringing two people together.

components.note: 土 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to earth, soil.
匽 (yǎn) shares the same base sound as "yàn", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 这条河上修建了一座堰。
example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo hé shàng xiùjiànle yī zuò yàn.
example.english: A dam was built on this river.
example.fact: The Dujiangyan (都江堰) irrigation system in Sichuan, whose name includes this very character, was built around 256 BCE and is still functioning today — one of the oldest continuously operating water-management systems in the world.

meanings: used in 彷徨[pang2 huang2] and 彷徉[pang2 yang2]

components.note: 彳 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to walking, stepping.
方 (fāng) shares the same base sound as "fǎng", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他在人生的十字路口感到彷徨。
example.pinyin: Tā zài rénshēng de shízì lùkǒu gǎndào pánghuáng.
example.english: He felt lost and hesitant at this crossroads in life.
example.fact: 彷徨 (to hesitate, to wander irresolutely) lent its name to a 1926 short-story collection by Lu Xun, one of modern China's most influential writers, reflecting the sense of doubt and searching that defined much of early 20th-century Chinese literature.

components.note: 鸟 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a bird.
婴 (yīng) is read identically to this character, "yīng" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 鹦鹉能模仿人说话的声音。
example.pinyin: Yīngwǔ néng mófǎng rén shuōhuà de shēngyīn.
example.english: Parrots can imitate the sound of human speech.
example.fact: Some parrot species, like the African grey parrot, can learn hundreds of words and even use them in appropriate context — studies on a famous research parrot named Alex suggested a level of cognitive and communicative ability rivaling young children.

components.note: 日 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the sun.
军 (jūn) no longer sounds close to "huī" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 夕阳的余晖洒满了大地。
example.pinyin: Xīyáng de yúhuī sǎmǎnle dàdì.
example.english: The lingering glow of the setting sun covered the land.
example.fact: 晖 is a common character in Chinese given names and poetic writing about light, distinct from the more everyday word 光 — it carries a softer, more literary connotation, often describing sunlight specifically at dawn or dusk.

etymologyHint: An ox 牛 with a tail 尾

components.note: Ox/cattle radical at the bottom — rhinoceroses were classified with cattle-like animals in the traditional radical system.

example.hanzi: 犀牛的皮肤非常厚。
example.pinyin: Xīniú de pífū fēicháng hòu.
example.english: A rhinoceros's skin is very thick.
example.fact: A rhinoceros's horn is made of keratin, the same protein found in human hair and fingernails — not bone or ivory as many people assume.

components.note: ⺼ is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to flesh, the body.
府 (fǔ) is read identically to this character, "fǔ" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 中医常常谈论五脏六腑。
example.pinyin: Zhōngyī chángcháng tánlùn wǔzàng liùfǔ.
example.english: Traditional Chinese medicine often discusses the five viscera and six internal organs.
example.fact: 五脏六腑 (the five viscera and six bowels) is a foundational concept in traditional Chinese medicine, organizing the body's internal organs into a systematic framework used in diagnosis for over two thousand years.

meanings: abbr. for Tianjin 天津 (also 津沽)

components.note: 氵 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to water.
古 (gǔ) shares the same base sound as "gū", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他喜欢沽酒会友。
example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan gūjiǔ huìyǒu.
example.english: He likes to buy wine and meet with friends.
example.fact: 沽 survives today mostly in the idiom 沽名钓誉 ('to fish for fame and reputation'), a critical phrase describing someone who acts virtuously only for the sake of public praise rather than genuine conviction.

meanings: used in 橄欖|橄榄[gan3 lan3]

components.note: 木 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to wood, a tree.
敢 (gǎn) is read identically to this character, "gǎn" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 地中海地区盛产橄榄油。
example.pinyin: Dìzhōnghǎi dìqū shèngchǎn gǎnlǎnyóu.
example.english: The Mediterranean region produces abundant olive oil.
example.fact: Olive trees are remarkably long-lived — some cultivated trees in the Mediterranean are documented to be well over 1,000 years old and still bear fruit today.

components.note: 扌 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the hand.
臽 (xiàn)'s own standalone reading is obscure today, so its exact historical closeness to "qiā" is hard to verify with confidence.

example.hanzi: 她轻轻掐断了一朵花。
example.pinyin: Tā qīngqīng qiāduànle yī duǒ huā.
example.english: She gently pinched off a flower.
example.fact: 掐 is also used in the phrase 掐指一算 ('to calculate on one's fingers'), traditionally describing a fortune-teller counting through the sexagenary cycle on their finger joints to make a prediction.

etymologyHint: Hands grasping 执 and tearing apart a dress 衣

components.note: Clothing radical — the character's meaning of disrespect or indecency ties back to imagery of clothes being pulled apart or handled carelessly.
Means 'to hold, to grasp'; contributes a reading only loosely related to modern 'xiè', and reinforces the sense of hands roughly grasping at clothing.

example.hanzi: 这种言论是对逝者的猥亵。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhǒng yánlùn shì duì shìzhě de wěixiè.
example.english: This kind of remark is disrespectful toward the deceased.
example.fact: 亵 appears in 亵渎 ('to defile, to profane'), a formal word used to describe disrespect toward something sacred — a religious belief, a memory, or an ideal — rather than everyday rudeness.

components.note: 齿 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to teeth.
禹 (yǔ) shares its rime/vowel with "qǔ", sharing the "ü" vowel — a reasonably close, though not exact, match.

example.hanzi: 吃糖太多容易导致龋齿。
example.pinyin: Chī táng tài duō róngyì dǎozhì qǔchǐ.
example.english: Eating too much candy can easily lead to tooth decay.
example.fact: Tooth decay is caused by bacteria in the mouth that feed on sugar and produce acid, which gradually dissolves the mineral structure of tooth enamel — a process that can be slowed simply by rinsing with water after eating sugary food.

meanings: used in 嗒然[ta4 ran2] and 嗒喪|嗒丧[ta4 sang4]

components.note: 口 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the mouth.
荅 (dá) shares the same base sound as "dā", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他听到这个消息后嗒然若失。
example.pinyin: Tā tīngdào zhège xiāoxi hòu dārán ruò shī.
example.english: After hearing the news, he seemed absent-minded and dejected.
example.fact: 嗒 is a comparatively rare character today, surviving mainly in the literary phrase 嗒然若失 ('looking blankly as if something were lost'), used to describe a moment of stunned disappointment.

components.note: 口 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the mouth.
且 (qiě) no longer sounds close to "jǔ" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 吃饭要慢慢咀嚼食物。
example.pinyin: Chīfàn yào mànmàn jǔjué shíwù.
example.english: When eating, you should chew your food slowly.
example.fact: Chewing food thoroughly, as this sentence advises, increases the surface area exposed to digestive enzymes in saliva, which is why nutritionists often recommend chewing each bite 20 to 30 times.

components.note: 礻 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a spirit or altar.
其 (qí) is read identically to this character, "qí" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 书信结尾常写“敬颂时祺”。
example.pinyin: Shūxìn jiéwěi cháng xiě “jìng sòng shí qí”.
example.english: Letters often close with the phrase 'respectfully wishing you well.'
example.fact: 祺 appears almost exclusively in formal letter-closing phrases and given names wishing good fortune, reflecting a tradition where certain characters were reserved almost entirely for polite, ceremonial language.

components.note: 钅 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to metal.
苗 (miáo) shares its rime/vowel with "máo", matching initial and tone, and a rime that differs only by a glide — a reasonably close, though not exact, match.

example.hanzi: 船员抛下锚，船停了下来。
example.pinyin: Chuányuán pāoxià máo, chuán tíngle xiàlái.
example.english: The sailor dropped the anchor, and the ship came to a stop.
example.fact: 锚 is written with the metal radical 钅 because, unlike the stone or wooden anchors of some ancient cultures, Chinese ships historically used iron anchors — a design still recognizable in anchors used today.

etymologyHint: A board 扁 made of bamboo 匸; 扁 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Means 'flat'; gives the reading and describes the flat shape of both the sign and the basket named by this character.

example.hanzi: 商店门口挂着一块牌匾。
example.pinyin: Shāngdiàn ménkǒu guàzhe yī kuài páibiǎn.
example.english: A signboard hangs at the entrance of the shop.
example.fact: 牌匾 (a horizontal signboard) traditionally hung above shop and temple entrances in China, often inscribed by famous calligraphers or officials — owning a board with prestigious calligraphy was itself a status symbol.

meanings: used with ping for ping pong
etymologyHint: A ball bouncing back and forth; compare 乒

components.note: Shares its shape with 乒; the pair of characters were invented together purely to imitate the bouncing sound of a ball, with a small stroke difference distinguishing the two syllables.

example.hanzi: 乒乓球是中国最受欢迎的运动之一。
example.pinyin: Pīngpāngqiú shì Zhōngguó zuì shòu huānyíng de yùndòng zhī yī.
example.english: Table tennis is one of the most popular sports in China.
example.fact: Since table tennis became an Olympic sport in 1988, China has won the large majority of all table tennis gold medals awarded across the Games, making it arguably the country's most dominant Olympic event.

components.note: 艹 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a plant, grass.
卒 (zú) only loosely echoes "cuì" — the initials z-/c- are related, but the rimes differ; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 这本书荟萃了他一生的研究成果。
example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū huìcuìle tā yīshēng de yánjiū chéngguǒ.
example.english: This book brings together the research achievements of his entire life.
example.fact: 萃 appears in the idiom 出类拔萃 ('to stand out from the crowd, to excel'), literally meaning to rise above a gathered cluster — a vivid image of a single stalk rising above a densely packed field of grass.

components.note: 贝 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to money, a cowrie shell.
台 (tái) no longer sounds close to "yí" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 他的错误决定贻误了整个项目。
example.pinyin: Tā de cuòwù juédìng yíwùle zhěnggè xiàngmù.
example.english: His mistaken decision set back the entire project.
example.fact: 贻 is written with the money/shell radical 贝 because in ancient China, cowrie shells were used as an early form of currency — many characters related to giving, trading, and value carry this radical.

meanings: to greet by raising clasped hands

components.note: 扌 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the hand.
咠 (qī)'s own standalone reading is obscure today, so its exact historical closeness to "yī" is hard to verify with confidence.

example.hanzi: 他向客人恭敬地作揖行礼。
example.pinyin: Tā xiàng kèrén gōngjìng de zuōyī xínglǐ.
example.english: He respectfully bowed with clasped hands to greet the guest.
example.fact: The 作揖 gesture — clasping the hands together and bowing slightly — was the standard formal greeting in imperial China for centuries, long predating the handshake that later spread from the West.

components.note: 见 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to seeing, sight.
虚 (xū) only loosely echoes "qù" — a similar rime, but the initials differ enough that this is only a loose match; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 他们面面相觑，不知所措。
example.pinyin: Tāmen miànmiàn xiāngqù, bùzhī suǒcuò.
example.english: They looked at each other in bewilderment, not knowing what to do.
example.fact: 面面相觑 ('to look at each other in stunned silence') is a common Chinese idiom for a group's shared moment of shock or confusion — 觑 itself, meaning 'to peer, to glance,' rarely appears outside this and a few similar set phrases.

components.note: Contributes to an old sense related to holding back words or refusing to give — connecting to 吝's meaning of stinginess.
Mouth radical — ties to the idea of being unwilling to speak or give.

example.hanzi: 他一向对钱很吝啬。
example.pinyin: Tā yīxiàng duì qián hěn lìnsè.
example.english: He has always been stingy with money.
example.fact: 吝啬 (stingy, miserly) pairs 吝 with 啬, an older character also meaning 'to be sparing' — a classic example of Chinese reinforcing a meaning by joining two characters that individually say almost the same thing.

components.note: 忄 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the heart, emotion.

焦 (jiāo)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "qiáo" (j- and q- are closely related sounds from the same historical consonant series, with a matching rime and tone), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 连续加班让他看起来很憔悴。
example.pinyin: Liánxù jiābān ràng tā kànqǐlái hěn qiáocuì.
example.english: Working overtime continuously has left him looking haggard.
example.fact: 憔悴 is one of the most common words in Chinese literature for describing physical exhaustion combined with emotional distress, appearing throughout classical poetry to depict lovesickness, grief, or hardship.

components.note: 羊 (yáng) only loosely echoes "qiāng" — sharing only the "-ang" rime; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 羌族是中国的一个少数民族。
example.pinyin: Qiāngzú shì Zhōngguó de yī gè shǎoshù mínzú.
example.english: The Qiang people are an ethnic minority in China.
example.fact: The Qiang ethnic group, mostly living in mountainous Sichuan, is one of China's oldest recorded ethnicities, mentioned in Chinese historical texts dating back over 3,000 years to the Shang dynasty.

components.note: 讠 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to speech, words.
每 (měi) no longer sounds close to "huì" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 老师耐心地教诲我们。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī nàixīn de jiàohuì wǒmen.
example.english: The teacher patiently instructs us.
example.fact: 教诲 (to instruct, to teach earnestly) carries a more solemn, respectful tone than the everyday word 教, and is traditionally used to describe the guidance given by a respected elder, teacher, or parent.

components.note: 石 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to stone.
乐 (lè) only loosely echoes "lì" — sharing only the initial "l-"; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 路上铺满了碎砾。
example.pinyin: Lùshang pūmǎnle suìlì.
example.english: The road was covered with gravel.
example.fact: 砾 is a component in geology terms like 砾石 (gravel/pebbles) and 砾岩 (conglomerate rock), which forms when gravel and pebbles become cemented together over long geological time.

components.note: 虫 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to an insect or small creature.
需 (xū) no longer sounds close to "rú" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 毛毛虫在叶子上蠕动。
example.pinyin: Máomaochóng zài yèzi shàng rúdòng.
example.english: The caterpillar wriggles along the leaf.
example.fact: 蠕动 (peristalsis, wriggling motion) is also the medical term for the wave-like muscle contractions that move food through the digestive system — the same word used for a caterpillar's motion describes a process happening inside your own body right now.

components.note: ⺼ is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to flesh, the body.
乂 (yì) no longer sounds close to "yáo" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 宴席上摆满了各种佳肴。
example.pinyin: Yànxí shàng bǎimǎnle gèzhǒng jiāyáo.
example.english: The banquet table was filled with all kinds of delicious dishes.
example.fact: 佳肴 (fine cuisine, delicacies) is a formal literary term still commonly used on Chinese restaurant menus and in travel writing, even though the plain word 菜 (dish) covers the same meaning in everyday speech.

components.note: 扌 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the hand.
尞 (liáo) shares the same base sound as "liāo", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 她撩起了窗边的帘子。
example.pinyin: Tā liāoqǐle chuāngbiān de liánzi.
example.english: She lifted up the curtain by the window.
example.fact: 撩 also appears in the modern slang term 撩妹 ('to flirt with a girl'), an example of an old character with a literal meaning of 'lifting or stirring up' taking on a completely new, informal meaning in contemporary internet slang.

components.note: 土 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to earth, soil.

丹 (dān)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "tān" (d- and t- are closely related alveolar sounds, with a matching rime and tone), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 地震导致一栋旧楼坍塌。
example.pinyin: Dìzhèn dǎozhì yī dòng jiù lóu tāntā.
example.english: The earthquake caused an old building to collapse.
example.fact: 坍塌 (to collapse) is written with the earth radical 土 in 坍, directly reflecting the character's meaning of a structure caving in toward the ground.

components.note: 禾 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to grain, a rice plant.
酉 (yǒu) no longer sounds close to "sū" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 这种点心口感十分酥脆。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhǒng diǎnxin kǒugǎn shífēn sūcuì.
example.english: This pastry has a very flaky, crispy texture.
example.fact: 酥 is written with the wine-jar radical 酉 and grain radical 禾 because it originally described a dairy product made from fermented milk, similar to clarified butter, before later broadening to mean any light, flaky texture.

components.note: 衣 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to clothing.
鸟 (niǎo) is read identically to this character, "niǎo" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 轻烟袅袅升起。
example.pinyin: Qīngyān niǎoniǎo shēngqǐ.
example.english: Light smoke curls gracefully upward.
example.fact: 袅袅 is a favorite word in classical Chinese poetry for describing gentle, drifting motion — used not only for smoke, but also for lingering musical notes and swaying willow branches.

components.note: 黑 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to black.
幼 (yòu) shares the same base sound as "yǒu", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 长期在户外工作让他皮肤黝黑。
example.pinyin: Chángqī zài hùwài gōngzuò ràng tā pífū yǒuhēi.
example.english: Working outdoors for a long time has made his skin deeply tanned.
example.fact: 黝黑 (dark, swarthy) combines 黝 with 黑 ('black') for emphasis — the character 黝 is written with the black radical 黑, one of relatively few Chinese color characters that never appears alone in modern speech.

components.note: 卑 (bēi) only loosely echoes "bǐ" — sharing only the initial "b-"; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 俾使众人得以周知。
example.pinyin: Bǐ shǐ zhòngrén déyǐ zhōuzhī.
example.english: So that everyone may be fully informed.
example.fact: 俾 today survives almost entirely in classical and highly formal written Chinese, functioning like the archaic English word 'whereby' — it is rarely, if ever, used in spoken conversation.

components.note: 女 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a woman.
焉 (yān) is read identically to this character, "yān" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 她嫣然一笑，十分动人。
example.pinyin: Tā yānrán yī xiào, shífēn dòngrén.
example.english: She smiled charmingly, utterly captivating.
example.fact: 嫣然一笑 ('a charming smile') is a classic phrase in Chinese literary description of beauty, and 嫣 itself is a popular character in Chinese women's given names for exactly this connotation of charm and radiance.

etymologyHint: An arched 弓 vault 穴; 弓 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Cave/hollow radical — evokes an arched, hollow space like the dome of the sky.
Means 'bow'; its curved shape visually echoes an arch, and it lends a reading close to, but not identical to, modern 'qióng'.

example.hanzi: 夜晚，苍穹布满了星星。
example.pinyin: Yèwǎn, cāngqióng bùmǎnle xīngxīng.
example.english: At night, the vast sky is filled with stars.
example.fact: 苍穹 ('the vast, vault-like sky') is a classical literary term picturing the heavens as a great dome — a poetic image echoed independently in many ancient cultures, including the Latin-derived word 'firmament.'

components.note: 禾 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to grain, a rice plant.
央 (yāng) is read identically to this character, "yāng" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 农民正在田里插秧。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín zhèngzài tián lǐ chāyāng.
example.english: The farmer is transplanting rice seedlings in the field.
example.fact: 插秧 (transplanting rice seedlings by hand) remains, even with modern machinery, one of the most labor-intensive steps of rice farming, and it inspired countless folk songs across rural China celebrating the rhythm of communal farm work.

components.note: 女 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a woman.
壬 (rén) shares the same base sound as "rèn", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 她怀孕，正处于妊娠期。
example.pinyin: Tā huáiyùn, zhèng chǔyú rènshēn qī.
example.english: She is pregnant, currently in the gestation period.
example.fact: 妊娠 is the formal medical term for pregnancy in Chinese, used in clinical and academic contexts, while 怀孕 is the everyday equivalent — a common pattern where Chinese medical vocabulary preserves more classical, literary characters.

components.note: 氵 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to water.
既 (jì) no longer sounds close to "gài" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 农民用河水灌溉农田。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín yòng héshuǐ guàngài nóngtián.
example.english: Farmers irrigate their fields with river water.
example.fact: Irrigation systems in ancient China, including networks fed by canals off the Yellow and Yangtze rivers, allowed farming to expand into otherwise dry regions and supported population growth that made China one of history's most populous civilizations.

components.note: 鸟 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a bird.
昔 (xī) no longer sounds close to "què" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 喜鹊在树枝上筑巢。
example.pinyin: Xǐquè zài shùzhī shàng zhùcháo.
example.english: The magpie builds its nest on the tree branch.
example.fact: In Chinese folklore, magpies (喜鹊) are said to form a bridge across the Milky Way once a year to reunite the separated lovers Niulang and Zhinü on Qixi, the Chinese equivalent of Valentine's Day.

etymologyHint: A hand 彐 holding a brush; compare 肀

components.note: The top portion pictures a hand gripping something upright — depicting a hand holding a writing brush, the character's original meaning.

example.hanzi: 聿是古代表示毛笔的字。
example.pinyin: Yù shì gǔdài biǎoshì máobǐ de zì.
example.english: 'Yu' is an ancient character representing a writing brush.
example.fact: 聿 is the ancient ancestor of the modern character 笔 (brush/pen) — over time, scribes added the bamboo radical 竹 on top of 聿 to specify that brush handles were made of bamboo, eventually producing today's 笔.

meanings: used in 疙瘩[ge1 da5] and 疙疸[ge1 da5]

components.note: 疒 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to sickness, illness.
乞 (qǐ) no longer sounds close to "gē" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 他脖子上长了一个疙瘩。
example.pinyin: Tā bózi shàng zhǎngle yī gè gēda.
example.english: He has developed a lump on his neck.
example.fact: 疙瘩 (a lump, pimple, or knot) also appears in the figurative expression 心里有疙瘩 ('to have a knot in one's heart'), describing an unresolved worry or grudge — a nice parallel to the English phrase 'a knot in your stomach.'

components.note: 艹 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a plant, grass.
磨 (mó) is read identically to this character, "mó" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 妈妈买了新鲜的蘑菇做汤。
example.pinyin: Māma mǎile xīnxiān de mógu zuò tāng.
example.english: Mom bought fresh mushrooms to make soup.
example.fact: Mushrooms are not plants at all — they belong to the fungus kingdom, a separate branch of life that gets its energy by absorbing nutrients rather than through photosynthesis.

components.note: Eye radical at the bottom of the older form, thought to derive from a component meaning 'to watch/examine,' unrelated in meaning to the modern anatomical sense of 睾.

example.hanzi: 睾丸是男性的生殖器官。
example.pinyin: Gāowán shì nánxìng de shēngzhí qìguān.
example.english: Testicles are a male reproductive organ.
example.fact: 睾丸 is the standard anatomical term used in Chinese biology and medical textbooks — 睾 rarely appears in any other word, a common pattern for characters whose entire modern use is confined to one specific technical term.

etymologyHint: The script 木 used by commoners 皆

components.note: Wood radical — 楷 originally named a specific tree (the Chinese pistachio); the sense of 'model, standard' developed later.
Means 'all, everyone'; contributes a reading only loosely related to modern 'kǎi'.

example.hanzi: 他的字写得很像楷书。
example.pinyin: Tā de zì xiě de hěn xiàng kǎishū.
example.english: His handwriting looks very much like regular script.
example.fact: 楷书 ('regular script') is the standardized, clearly-legible style of Chinese calligraphy that emerged around the 2nd–3rd century CE and remains the basis for printed Chinese fonts and the model style taught to schoolchildren today.

components.note: 酉 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to wine, fermentation.

孝 (xiào)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "jiào" (x- and j- are related sounds from the same historical consonant series, with a matching rime and tone), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 面团需要经过发酵才能变松软。
example.pinyin: Miàntuán xūyào jīngguò fājiào cáinéng biàn sōngruǎn.
example.english: Dough needs to go through fermentation to become soft and fluffy.
example.fact: Fermentation, described by this character's core word 发酵, is powered by yeast microorganisms that convert sugars into carbon dioxide gas — the same gas bubbles that make bread rise and give beer its fizz.

components.note: 艹 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a plant, grass.
如 (rú) is read identically to this character, "rú" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 他茹苦含辛地把孩子养大。
example.pinyin: Tā rúkǔ hánxīn de bǎ háizi yǎng dà.
example.english: He endured great hardship to raise the child.
example.fact: 茹苦含辛 ('to swallow bitterness and endure hardship') pairs 茹, meaning 'to endure/eat,' with imagery of literally consuming bitterness — a vivid metaphor for enduring suffering silently over a long period.

components.note: 钅 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to metal.
辛 (xīn) is read identically to this character, "xīn" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 锌是一种重要的微量元素。
example.pinyin: Xīn shì yī zhǒng zhòngyào de wēiliàng yuánsù.
example.english: Zinc is an important trace element.
example.fact: Zinc is essential to human health in small amounts — it plays a role in immune function and wound healing, but like several trace metals, it becomes toxic in excessive doses.

meanings: short name for Yunnan 雲南|云南[Yun2 nan2]

components.note: 氵 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to water.
真 (zhēn) no longer sounds close to "diān" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 滇是云南省的简称。
example.pinyin: Diān shì Yúnnán shěng de jiǎnchēng.
example.english: 'Dian' is the short name for Yunnan province.
example.fact: Yunnan's short name 滇 comes from ancient Lake Dian (滇池), near the provincial capital Kunming, around which one of southern China's earliest Bronze Age kingdoms, the Dian Kingdom, flourished over 2,000 years ago.

meanings: used in 輾轉|辗转[zhan3 zhuan3]

components.note: 车 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a cart, a vehicle.
展 (zhǎn) no longer sounds close to "niǎn" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 他在床上辗转反侧，难以入睡。
example.pinyin: Tā zài chuáng shàng zhǎnzhuǎn fǎncè, nányǐ rùshuì.
example.english: He tossed and turned in bed, unable to fall asleep.
example.fact: 辗转反侧 ('tossing and turning') is a phrase that appears as early as the 'Book of Songs' (诗经), China's oldest poetry collection, describing a lovesick person's sleeplessness nearly 3,000 years ago.

components.note: 糸 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to silk, thread.
算 (suàn)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "zuǎn" (s- and z- are closely related sounds, with a matching rime), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 学者们花费数十年编纂这部辞典。
example.pinyin: Xuézhěmen huāfèi shùshí nián biānzuǎn zhè bù cídiǎn.
example.english: Scholars spent decades compiling this dictionary.
example.fact: 编纂 (to compile, especially a major reference work) describes the process behind China's historic encyclopedic projects, such as the Yongle Encyclopedia of the early 1400s, one of the largest encyclopedias ever assembled before the digital age.

components.note: Two stacked 'earth/soil' components together depict a tall, pointed jade or stone tablet — the object 圭 originally named.

example.hanzi: 古人常以圭臬比喻行事的准则。
example.pinyin: Gǔrén cháng yǐ guīniè bǐyù xíngshì de zhǔnzé.
example.english: Ancient people often used 'guinie' as a metaphor for the standards guiding one's conduct.
example.fact: 圭 originally named a pointed jade tablet used by nobles in ancient ceremonies; the idiom 圭臬 ('standard, guiding principle') pairs it with 臬, an ancient sundial marker, combining two old measuring tools into a metaphor for a moral or practical standard.

components.note: 巾 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to cloth.
曼 (màn) is read identically to this character, "màn" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 床边挂着一层薄薄的幔帐。
example.pinyin: Chuángbiān guàzhe yī céng bóbó de màn zhàng.
example.english: A thin curtain hangs by the bedside.
example.fact: 幔 traditionally described the light cloth curtains hung around a canopy bed in imperial-era Chinese homes — a design meant to provide privacy and keep out mosquitoes in a bedroom without solid walls dividing the space.

components.note: 衣 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to clothing.
保 (bǎo) shares the same base sound as "bāo", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 老师在报告里褒扬了他的努力。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī zài bàogào lǐ bāoyángle tā de nǔlì.
example.english: The teacher praised his effort in the report.
example.fact: 褒 is the direct opposite of 贬 (to belittle, to demote) in the common pairing 褒贬 ('praise and criticism'), a compound frequently used to describe balanced or mixed feedback, as in 褒贬不一 ('opinions are mixed').

components.note: 扌 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the hand.
