奏 (zòu) is read identically to this character, "zòu" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 他因为撒谎而挨了一顿揍。
example.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi sāhuǎng ér áile yī dùn zòu.
example.english: He got a beating for lying.
example.fact: 揍 is a distinctly colloquial character, almost never appearing in formal writing — its everyday, spoken-register tone contrasts with the many literary characters found elsewhere at this frequency range.

components.note: 讠 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to speech, words.
非 (fēi) shares the same base sound as "fěi", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他因散布谣言诽谤别人而被起诉。
example.pinyin: Tā yīn sànbù yáoyán fěibàng biérén ér bèi qǐsù.
example.english: He was sued for spreading rumors and slandering others.
example.fact: 诽谤 (slander, defamation) is a legally defined term in Chinese law just as it is in most legal systems worldwide — falsely damaging someone's reputation through speech has been recognized as a punishable wrong across a wide range of legal traditions.

meanings: used in 倔強|倔强[jue2 jiang4]
etymologyHint: Someone 亻 who does not bend 屈; 屈 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Person radical — describes a personality trait.
Means 'to bend, to submit'; provides a reading close to but not identical to modern 'jué', and the meaning 'someone who refuses to bend' plays directly off 屈's sense of bending.

example.hanzi: 他这个人很倔强，很难说服。
example.pinyin: Tā zhège rén hěn juéjiàng, hěn nán shuōfú.
example.english: This person is very stubborn and hard to persuade.
example.fact: 倔强 (stubborn, unyielding) can carry either a negative or a subtly admiring tone in Chinese depending on context — describing someone as 倔强 sometimes praises their unbending determination rather than simply criticizing their inflexibility.

components.note: ⺼ is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to flesh, the body.
非 (fēi) shares the same base sound as "féi", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 长时间站立让他的腓部肌肉酸痛。
example.pinyin: Chángshíjiān zhànlì ràng tā de féibù jīròu suāntòng.
example.english: Standing for a long time made his calf muscles sore.
example.fact: 腓 names the calf of the leg in classical and medical Chinese; the word 腓肠肌 ('gastrocnemius,' the main calf muscle) is still the standard anatomical term used in Chinese medicine and biology today.

meanings: used in 倉頡|仓颉[Cang1 Jie2]

components.note: 页 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the head.
吉 (jí) shares its rime/vowel with "jié", matching initial and tone, with a rime that has shifted slightly — a reasonably close, though not exact, match.

example.hanzi: 传说仓颉创造了汉字。
example.pinyin: Chuánshuō Cāngjié chuàngzàole Hànzì.
example.english: Legend says Cang Jie created Chinese characters.
example.fact: Cang Jie (仓颉) is the legendary figure credited in Chinese mythology with inventing writing, said to have been inspired by the tracks of birds and animals — a foundational story explaining the origin of the very characters used to tell it.

etymologyHint: A metal 钅 tool 助; 助 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Metal radical — a hoe blade is made of metal.
Means 'to help'; contributes a reading only loosely close to modern 'chú', with the tool itself 'helping' in farm labor.

example.hanzi: 农夫拿着锄头翻地。
example.pinyin: Nóngfū názhe chútou fāndì.
example.english: The farmer turns over the soil with a hoe.
example.fact: 锄头 (the hoe) remained the primary tool for turning soil in small Chinese farms for thousands of years, and the idiom 锄强扶弱 ('to root out the strong and support the weak') extends the hoe's literal digging action into a metaphor for fighting injustice.

components.note: 口 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the mouth.

真 (zhēn)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "chēn" (zh- and ch- are closely related retroflex sounds, with a matching rime and tone), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 她因为被冤枉而嗔怒不已。
example.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi bèi yuānwǎng ér chēnnù bùyǐ.
example.english: She was furious at being wrongly accused.
example.fact: 嗔 is a term borrowed into Chinese Buddhism to name one of the 'Three Poisons' (三毒) — greed, hatred (嗔), and ignorance — considered the three root causes of human suffering in Buddhist philosophy.

etymologyHint: A yellow 黄 mineral 石; 黄 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Stone/mineral radical — sulfur occurs naturally as a mineral.
Means 'yellow'; provides the reading and also describes the mineral's natural color.

example.hanzi: 火山附近常能找到硫磺。
example.pinyin: Huǒshān fùjìn cháng néng zhǎodào liúhuáng.
example.english: Sulfur can often be found near volcanoes.
example.fact: Sulfur deposits commonly form around volcanic vents, and the mineral's yellow color, referenced directly in this character's phonetic component 黄, has made it visually recognizable at active volcanic sites for centuries.

components.note: 扌 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the hand.
赞 (zàn) shares the same base sound as "zǎn", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他省吃俭用，攒了不少钱。
example.pinyin: Tā shěngchī jiǎnyòng, zǎnle bù shǎo qián.
example.english: He lived frugally and saved up quite a bit of money.
example.fact: 攒钱 ('to save up money') uses 攒 specifically for gradually accumulating something bit by bit over time, distinct from 存钱, which more neutrally means 'to deposit or keep money.'

components.note: 疒 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to sickness, illness.
荅 (dá) shares the same base sound as "da", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他脸上长了一个疙瘩。
example.pinyin: Tā liǎn shàng zhǎngle yī gè gēda.
example.english: A pimple grew on his face.
example.fact: 瘩 almost never appears alone — it exists in modern Chinese exclusively as the second syllable of 疙瘩, a compound naming a small lump, bump, or knot, whether physical or figurative.

meanings: used in 霹靂|霹雳[pi1 li4]

components.note: 雨 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to rain.
历 (lì) is read identically to this character, "lì" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 远处传来一阵霹雳般的雷声。
example.pinyin: Yuǎnchù chuánlái yī zhèn pīlì bān de léishēng.
example.english: A thunderclap-like sound came rumbling from the distance.
example.fact: 雳 exists in modern Chinese only as the second character of 霹雳 ('crashing thunder'), a compound word describing the loud, cracking type of thunder that follows a nearby lightning strike, as opposed to the low rolling rumble of distant thunder.

components.note: 口 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the mouth.
幺 (yāo) is read identically to this character, "yāo" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 小贩在街边大声吆喝。
example.pinyin: Xiǎofàn zài jiē biān dàshēng yāohe.
example.english: The street vendor shouted loudly by the roadside.
example.fact: 吆喝 (to shout, to hawk goods loudly) describes a vanishing tradition of Chinese street vendors calling out distinctive, often musical cries to advertise their goods — a practice now studied by folklorists as a form of urban oral heritage.

components.note: 忄 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the heart, emotion.
束 (shù) no longer sounds close to "sǒng" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 那个故事让人毛骨悚然。
example.pinyin: Nàge gùshì ràng rén máogǔ sǒngrán.
example.english: That story sent chills down people's spines.
example.fact: 毛骨悚然 ('hair-raising, spine-chilling') describes the same physiological reflex as the English phrase 'goosebumps' — tiny muscles at the base of body hair contract involuntarily in response to fear or cold, a reflex left over from mammalian ancestors whose fur would puff up for warmth or to look larger to predators.

components.note: 土 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to earth, soil.
敦 (dūn) is read identically to this character, "dūn" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 河边立着几个石墩。
example.pinyin: Hébiān lìzhe jǐ gè shídūn.
example.english: A few stone piers stand by the riverbank.
example.fact: 石墩 (stone piers or blocks) were traditionally used in Chinese architecture as sturdy bases to raise wooden pillars off damp ground, protecting the wood from rot in humid climates.

components.note: Grain component within the character, part of an old picture of a ceremonial vessel holding sacrificial grain and silk offerings.
Silk/thread radical, also part of the old picture of a ritual vessel bound with silk cords for offerings.

example.hanzi: 彝族有着独特的火把节。
example.pinyin: Yízú yǒuzhe dútè de huǒbǎjié.
example.english: The Yi ethnic group has a unique Torch Festival.
example.fact: The Yi people's Torch Festival (火把节), celebrated mainly in Yunnan and Sichuan, involves villagers lighting large bonfires and torches at night to ward off misfortune and pray for a good harvest — one of the most visually striking ethnic festivals in China.

etymologyHint: A fire 夂 burning and giving off smoke

components.note: The enclosing box shape pictures the outer wall or shaft of a chimney.
In the ancient form, this element represented rising smoke or flame escaping through the opening — the visual core of the character's meaning.

example.hanzi: 屋顶上冒出了烟囱的黑烟。
example.pinyin: Wūdǐng shàng màochūle yāncōng de hēiyān.
example.english: Black smoke rose from the chimney on the roof.
example.fact: 囱 by itself is rare in modern Chinese, appearing almost only inside 烟囱 (chimney) — but it is also hidden inside the far more common character 窗 (window), which adds the cave/hole radical 穴 on top of 囱 to depict an opening that lets light in, just as a chimney lets smoke out.

meanings: used in 逍遙|逍遥[xiao1 yao2]

components.note: 辶 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to walking, movement.
肖 (xiào) shares the same base sound as "xiāo", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他喜欢在山间逍遥自在地散步。
example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan zài shānjiān xiāoyáo zìzài de sànbù.
example.english: He likes to stroll freely and carefree among the mountains.
example.fact: 逍遥 (carefree, unfettered) is central to Daoist philosophy — the very first chapter of Zhuangzi, a foundational Daoist text from around the 4th century BCE, is titled '逍遥游' ('Free and Easy Wandering'), celebrating a life unburdened by social convention.

components.note: 车 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a cart, a vehicle.
耴 (zhé) is read identically to this character, "zhé" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 他动辄发脾气，让人很难相处。
example.pinyin: Tā dòngzhé fā píqì, ràng rén hěn nán xiāngchǔ.
example.english: He loses his temper at the slightest thing, making him hard to get along with.
example.fact: 辄 survives today almost entirely inside the word 动辄 ('at the drop of a hat, readily'), used to criticize someone who reacts to minor triggers with an outsized response.

components.note: 木 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to wood, a tree.
危 (wēi) shares the same base sound as "wéi", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 船上的桅杆在风中摇晃。
example.pinyin: Chuán shàng de wéigǎn zài fēngzhōng yáohuàng.
example.english: The ship's mast sways in the wind.
example.fact: Before steam power, tall sailing ships sometimes had masts over 60 meters high — taller than most buildings of their era — engineered to catch enough wind to move thousands of tons of cargo across oceans.

components.note: 亻 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a person.
严 (yán) shares the same base sound as "yǎn", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他神情俨然，令人不敢靠近。
example.pinyin: Tā shénqíng yǎnrán, lìng rén bùgǎn kàojìn.
example.english: His expression was so solemn that people dared not approach.
example.fact: 俨然 can mean both 'solemn, dignified' and, in a different usage, 'as if, seemingly exactly like' (as in 俨然一位专家, 'looking just like an expert') — a character whose two common meanings can seem almost unrelated at first glance.

etymologyHint: To spin thread 纟 into order 仑; 仑 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Silk/thread radical — 纶 originally named a fine silk thread or ribbon.
Contributes a reading close to but not identical to modern 'lún', and carries a sense of 'order, sequence' echoed in 纶's other meaning of orderly statecraft (经纶).

example.hanzi: 这件衣服是涤纶材质的。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu shì dílún cáizhì de.
example.english: This piece of clothing is made of polyester.
example.fact: 涤纶 is the Chinese name for polyester, one of the world's most widely used synthetic fibers — the character 纶, once used only for fine silk thread in classical texts, was repurposed in the 20th century to name this entirely new man-made material.

components.note: 忄 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the heart, emotion.
季 (jì) is read identically to this character, "jì" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 想到考试，她心里一阵悸动。
example.pinyin: Xiǎngdào kǎoshì, tā xīnlǐ yī zhèn jìdòng.
example.english: Thinking about the exam, her heart gave a nervous flutter.
example.fact: 心悸 (heart palpitations) is both an everyday word for feeling one's heart race with emotion and a specific medical term describing an irregular or unusually strong heartbeat that doctors evaluate as a possible symptom of underlying conditions.

components.note: 歹 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to death, misfortune.
央 (yāng) is read identically to this character, "yāng" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 一场大雨给全城带来了殃害。
example.pinyin: Yī chǎng dàyǔ gěi quánchéng dàiláile yānghài.
example.english: A heavy rainstorm brought disaster to the whole city.
example.fact: 殃 appears in the idiom 城门失火，殃及池鱼 ('when the city gate catches fire, even the fish in the moat suffer'), a classical proverb warning that unrelated parties can be harmed as collateral damage from a disaster they had nothing to do with.

components.note: 巾 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to cloth.
贞 (zhēn) shares its rime/vowel with "zhèng", matching initial, with rimes that are similar nasal finals but not identical — a reasonably close, though not exact, match.

example.hanzi: 这张照片只是电影的一帧画面。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhāng zhàopiàn zhǐshì diànyǐng de yī zhēn huàmiàn.
example.english: This photo is just a single frame from the movie.
example.fact: 帧 is the standard technical unit for a single still image in a video, which is why frame rates are measured in Chinese as 帧/秒 ('frames per second') — the same measurement used worldwide for video and animation smoothness.

components.note: 亻 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a person.
利 (lì) is read identically to this character, "lì" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 这个孩子很伶俐，学东西很快。
example.pinyin: Zhège háizi hěn línglì, xué dōngxi hěn kuài.
example.english: This child is very clever, learning things quickly.
example.fact: 伶俐 (clever, nimble-witted) is most often used to praise children specifically, describing quick-mindedness in a way that carries a warmer, more affectionate tone than the more neutral word 聪明 ('intelligent').

components.note: 纟 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to silk, thread.
奇 (qí) shares the same base sound as "qǐ", differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 她穿着一件绮丽的长裙。
example.pinyin: Tā chuānzhe yī jiàn qǐlì de chángqún.
example.english: She wore a gorgeously beautiful long dress.
example.fact: 绮 is written with the silk radical 纟 because it originally named a type of fine, patterned silk fabric reserved for the wealthy in ancient China — the character's later meaning of 'gorgeous, splendid' grew directly from this luxurious cloth.

components.note: 衤 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to clothing.
旦 (dàn)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "tǎn" (d- and t- are closely related sounds, with a matching rime), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 父母总是袒护自己的孩子。
example.pinyin: Fùmǔ zǒngshì tǎnhù zìjǐ de háizi.
example.english: Parents always shield and favor their own children.
example.fact: 袒护 (to shield, to be biased in favor of) comes from 袒's literal meaning of baring one's chest — the figurative sense likely developed from the image of physically stepping in front of someone to protect them, exposing oneself to danger instead.

etymologyHint: A grain 米 seed 子; 子 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Grain/rice radical — a seed grows into a grain-bearing plant.
Means 'child, offspring'; gives the reading and reinforces the idea of a seed as the 'offspring' of a plant.

example.hanzi: 农民在田里播下了种籽。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín zài tián lǐ bōxiàle zhǒngzǐ.
example.english: The farmer sowed seeds in the field.
example.fact: 籽 is a comparatively modern character used specifically for plant seeds intended for planting, in contrast to 子 alone, which carries dozens of unrelated meanings from 'child' to 'small object' — 籽 was created to disambiguate the agricultural sense.

components.note: Relates to an old sense of offering or presenting something, tied to 孰's ancient meaning involving ritual food or maturity.

example.hanzi: 孰是孰非，众人各有看法。
example.pinyin: Shú shì shú fēi, zhòngrén gè yǒu kànfǎ.
example.english: As to who is right and who is wrong, everyone has their own opinion.
example.fact: 孰 is a classical Chinese question word roughly equivalent to 'who' or 'which,' still recognizable today mainly through the idiom 是可忍，孰不可忍 ('if this can be tolerated, what cannot be?'), attributed to Confucius in the Analects.

etymologyHint: With a pure 素 heart 忄; 素 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Heart radical — 愫 names an inner, heartfelt feeling.
Means 'plain, unadorned'; provides the reading and reinforces the idea of a sincere, unembellished emotion.

example.hanzi: 他心中藏着一份深深的情愫。
example.pinyin: Tā xīnzhōng cángzhe yī fèn shēnshēn de qíngsù.
example.english: He harbors a deep, tender feeling in his heart.
example.fact: 愫 survives in modern Mandarin almost entirely in the word 情愫 ('a tender, budding emotion,' often romantic), a poetic term favored in literature and lyrics over more blunt words for 'feelings' or 'emotion.'

components.note: 扌 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the hand.
半 (bàn) is read identically to this character, "bàn" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 她把沙拉和调料拌在一起。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ shālā hé tiáoliào bàn zài yīqǐ.
example.english: She mixed the salad together with the dressing.
example.fact: 拌 is the character used in 凉拌 (cold-mixed dishes), a whole category of Chinese cold appetizers made by tossing raw or blanched vegetables with sauce rather than cooking them with heat.

components.note: 木 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to wood, a tree.
登 (dēng) only loosely echoes "chéng" — sharing only the "-eng" rime; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 冬天多吃橙子有助于补充维生素C。
example.pinyin: Dōngtiān duō chī chéngzi yǒuzhùyú bǔchōng wéishēngsù C.
example.english: Eating more oranges in winter helps supplement vitamin C.
example.fact: One medium orange provides more than a full day's recommended intake of vitamin C for most adults, which is part of why citrus fruits became historically famous for preventing scurvy on long sea voyages.

components.note: 旦 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to dawn.
既 (jì) is read identically to this character, "jì" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 这份名单暨往届获奖者一并公布。
example.pinyin: Zhè fèn míngdān jì wǎngjiè huòjiǎngzhě yī bìng gōngbù.
example.english: This list, along with past award winners, is announced together.
example.fact: 暨 appears in the name of Jinan University (暨南大学) in Guangzhou, one of China's oldest universities catering to overseas Chinese students — the character conveys a formal sense of 'reaching out to' or 'together with' distant places.

components.note: An 'action' radical often seen in characters describing ongoing activity, fitting 敖's original meaning of wandering or rambling about.

example.hanzi: 敖是一个不常见的姓氏。
example.pinyin: Áo shì yī gè bù chángjiàn de xìngshì.
example.english: Ao is an uncommon surname.
example.fact: 敖 today functions mainly as a surname and as a phonetic component inside more common characters like 傲 ('proud, arrogant') and 遨 ('to roam, to travel freely'), both of which build on 敖's ancient meaning of wandering leisurely.

components.note: 敖 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to leisurely wandering, extended here to something excessive.
贝 (bèi) no longer sounds close to "zhuì" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 这份报告有很多累赘的细节。
example.pinyin: Zhè fèn bàogào yǒu hěnduō léizhuì de xìjié.
example.english: This report has a lot of superfluous details.
example.fact: 累赘 (superfluous, cumbersome) is often used to describe writing padded with unnecessary detail — advice to avoid being 累赘 appears frequently in Chinese writing and editing guides, much like English advice to 'cut the clutter.'

etymologyHint: To choose 夬 by hand 扌; 夬 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Hand radical — choosing or picking out involves the hand.
Provides a reading close to but not identical to modern 'jué'; originally related to the idea of breaking off or separating something, echoing the act of picking one option out from others.

example.hanzi: 面对两个选择，他必须做出抉择。
example.pinyin: Miànduì liǎng gè xuǎnzé, tā bìxū zuòchū juézé.
example.english: Facing two options, he had to make a decision.
example.fact: 抉择 (a difficult decision, a critical choice) carries more weight than the everyday word 选择, and is typically reserved in Chinese for decisions with serious, often irreversible, consequences.

components.note: 氵 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to water.
於 (yū) is read identically to this character, "yū" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 河底积满了淤泥。
example.pinyin: Hédǐ jīmǎnle yūní.
example.english: The riverbed is filled with silt.
example.fact: 淤泥 (silt, mud sediment) accumulates in slow-moving or dammed rivers as suspended particles settle out of the water — over centuries this process built the fertile floodplains that made river valleys like the Yellow River basin ideal for early agriculture.

components.note: 刂 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a knife, cutting.
束 (shù) no longer sounds close to "lá" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 他说话总是乖剌，让人难以相处。
example.pinyin: Tā shuōhuà zǒngshì guāilá, ràng rén nányǐ xiāngchǔ.
example.english: He always speaks in a contrary, unreasonable way, making him hard to get along with.
example.fact: 剌 is a rare character today, distinguished from the far more common 刺 ('to stab, to prick') by only a single stroke — the two are frequently confused even by native speakers, since 剌 appears almost exclusively in the classical compound 乖剌 ('perverse, contrary').

components.note: 女 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a woman.
昌 (chāng) is read identically to this character, "chāng" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 旧社会里娼妓的处境十分悲惨。
example.pinyin: Jiù shèhuì lǐ chāngjì de chǔjìng shífēn bēicǎn.
example.english: In the old society, the situation of prostitutes was extremely tragic.
example.fact: 娼 is written with the woman radical 女, part of a broader historical pattern in the Chinese writing system where many characters describing women's social roles — some neutral, some pejorative — were built on this single radical, reflecting the gender assumptions embedded in the script's ancient origins.

meanings: used in 顓頊|颛顼[Zhuan1 xu1]
used in 頊頊|顼顼[xu1 xu1]

components.note: Jade radical (identical in form to the character for 'king') — many jade-related characters use this shape, though the connection to 顼's specific meaning is unclear.
Head radical, appearing in many characters related to the head or face.

example.hanzi: 颛顼是中国古代传说中的帝王。
example.pinyin: Zhuānxū shì Zhōngguó gǔdài chuánshuō zhōng de dìwáng.
example.english: Zhuanxu is a legendary emperor in ancient Chinese mythology.
example.fact: 颛顼 (Zhuanxu) is one of the legendary 'Five Emperors' of Chinese mythology, said to have ruled around 2500 BCE and to be a grandson of the Yellow Emperor — a foundational figure in China's origin stories, though 顼 itself appears almost nowhere outside his name.

meanings: used in the names of various herbaceous plants

components.note: 艹 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a plant, grass.
癸 (guǐ)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "kuí" (g- and k- are closely related velar sounds, with a matching rime), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 向日葵总是朝着太阳的方向生长。
example.pinyin: Xiàngrìkuí zǒngshì cháozhe tàiyáng de fāngxiàng shēngzhǎng.
example.english: Sunflowers always grow facing toward the sun.
example.fact: Young sunflowers track the sun's movement across the sky through a process called heliotropism, but once they mature and flower, most stop tracking and settle into facing a fixed eastward direction.

components.note: 口 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the mouth.
农 (nóng) is read identically to this character, "nóng" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 他们在角落里咕哝了几句。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zài jiǎoluò lǐ gūnóngle jǐ jù.
example.english: They muttered a few words in the corner.
example.fact: 咕哝 (to mutter, to grumble under one's breath) is a phonetically expressive word — both characters share the mouth radical 口, a visual pattern common across Chinese words that describe indistinct, low-volume speech sounds.

components.note: 酉 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to wine, fermentation.
甘 (gān)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "hān" (g- and h- are related guttural sounds, with a matching rime and tone), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 两位棋手正在酣战。
example.pinyin: Liǎng wèi qíshǒu zhèngzài hānzhàn.
example.english: The two chess players are locked in an intense battle.
example.fact: 酣 originally described the state of being pleasantly intoxicated from wine, and later broadened into a metaphor for anything happening at its most intense or fullest stage — as in 酣战 ('a battle in full swing') or 酣睡 ('deep sleep').

components.note: 林 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a forest.
鹿 (lù) is read identically to this character, "lù" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 村庄坐落在山麓之下。
example.pinyin: Cūnzhuāng zuòluò zài shānlù zhīxià.
example.english: The village is located at the foot of the mountain.
example.fact: 麓 is written with the forest radical 林 above the deer radical 鹿, reflecting how the forested foothills of a mountain — the character's meaning — were traditionally understood as the habitat where deer and other forest wildlife roamed.

components.note: 钅 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to metal.
本 (běn) only loosely echoes "bō" — sharing only the initial "b-"; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 僧人手持一个化缘的钵。
example.pinyin: Sēngrén shǒuchí yī gè huàyuán de bō.
example.english: The monk holds an alms bowl for begging.
example.fact: The alms bowl (钵) is one of the most important possessions in Buddhist monastic tradition, and the phrase 传衣钵 ('to pass on the robe and bowl') describes a master formally naming a successor to inherit their teachings — now used more broadly in Chinese to mean 'to pass down a legacy.'

meanings: used in 瑯琊|琅琊[Lang2 ya2]

components.note: 王 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to jade.
良 (liáng) shares its rime/vowel with "láng", matching initial and tone, and a rime that differs only by a glide — a reasonably close, though not exact, match.

example.hanzi: 商店里的商品琳琅满目。
example.pinyin: Shāngdiàn lǐ de shāngpǐn línláng mǎnmù.
example.english: The store's merchandise is dazzling to behold.
example.fact: 琳琅满目 ('a dazzling array meeting the eye') originally described the pleasant tinkling sound of jade ornaments knocking together — 琅 itself refers to that sound, before the phrase broadened to describe any visually overwhelming, attractive display of goods.

meanings: to winnow; to toss up and down

components.note: ⺮ is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to bamboo.
皮 (pí) no longer sounds close to "bǒ" in modern Mandarin — the phonetic link reflects an older pronunciation that has since drifted apart.

example.hanzi: 农民用簸箕把谷物中的杂物筛出去。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín yòng bòjī bǎ gǔwù zhōng de záwù shāi chūqù.
example.english: The farmer uses a winnowing basket to sift impurities out of the grain.
example.fact: A 簸箕 (winnowing basket) works by tossing grain into the air so a breeze — natural or fan-generated — blows away the lighter chaff while the heavier grain falls back into the basket, a technique used across farming cultures worldwide for thousands of years before mechanical threshers existed.

etymologyHint: A plant stalk with a sagging head

example.hanzi: 秋天，田里的禾苗已经成熟了。
example.pinyin: Qiūtiān, tián lǐ de hémiáo yǐjīng chéngshú le.
example.english: In autumn, the grain seedlings in the field have already ripened.
example.fact: 禾 is one of the 214 traditional radicals of the Chinese writing system and, as a pictograph of a drooping grain stalk, is the root component inside dozens of common agricultural characters, including 秋 (autumn), 秒 (second, originally the tiny bristle-like tip of a grain stalk), and 种 (to plant).

meanings: one twenty-fourth of a Chinese ounce (liang)
twenty-fourth part of a tael (2 or 3 grams)

components.note: 钅 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to metal.
朱 (zhū) is read identically to this character, "zhū" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 他为人处世总是锱铢必较。
example.pinyin: Tā wéirén chǔshì zǒngshì zīzhū bìjiào.
example.english: He is always fussing over the smallest details in his dealings with others.
example.fact: 锱铢必较 ('to fuss over every ounce') refers to two ancient, extremely small units of weight — 锱 and 铢 — with 24 铢 making up just one 两 (tael), roughly 37 grams; the idiom uses these tiny measures to criticize excessive stinginess over trivial amounts.

meanings: piece of jade with hole in it

components.note: 玉 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to jade.
辟 (bì) is read identically to this character, "bì" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 这块璧玉雕刻得十分精美。
example.pinyin: Zhè kuài bìyù diāokè de shífēn jīngměi.
example.english: This jade disc is exquisitely carved.
example.fact: The idiom 完璧归赵 ('the jade disc returned intact to Zhao') comes from a famous 3rd-century BCE story of a diplomat who outwitted a rival state to bring a priceless jade disc safely home — the phrase is still used today to mean returning something valuable undamaged.

components.note: 女 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a woman.

辰 (chén)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "shēn" (ch- and sh- are closely related retroflex sounds, with a matching rime and tone), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 她已经怀孕娠动了。
example.pinyin: Tā yǐjīng huáiyùn shēndòng le.
example.english: She is already pregnant and feeling movement.
example.fact: 娠 is the second character of 妊娠 (gestation/pregnancy), the formal medical term — like many characters confined to specialized vocabulary, 娠 almost never stands alone in everyday conversation.

etymologyHint: A hand 彐 holding a bamboo broom 丰

components.note: This shape depicts a hand gripping a handle, shown holding the broom's bristles pictured above it — together forming the image of a hand-held broom.

example.hanzi: 天文学家观测到了一颗彗星。
example.pinyin: Tiānwénxuéjiā guāncè dàole yī kē huìxīng.
example.english: Astronomers observed a comet.
example.fact: 彗星 ('comet') uses this character because a comet's glowing tail resembles a broom sweeping across the night sky — the same visual metaphor that gave English comets their name too, from the Greek 'kometes,' meaning 'long-haired star.'

meanings: to sigh in regret or pity

components.note: 忄 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the heart, emotion.
宛 (wǎn) is read identically to this character, "wǎn" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 得知老友离世，他深感惋惜。
example.pinyin: Dézhī lǎoyǒu líshì, tā shēngǎn wǎnxī.
example.english: Learning of his old friend's passing, he felt deep regret.
example.fact: 惋惜 (to feel regretful sympathy) is typically used for regret over someone else's misfortune or loss, distinct from 后悔 (regret over one's own past actions or mistakes) — a distinction English 'regret' doesn't always make as clearly.

components.note: ⺼ is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to flesh, the body.
夜 (yè) is read identically to this character, "yè" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 他把体温计夹在腋下测量体温。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ tǐwēnjì jiā zài yèxià cèliáng tǐwēn.
example.english: He tucked the thermometer under his armpit to measure his body temperature.
example.fact: Measuring body temperature under the armpit (腋下), as in this sentence, is a common method in China and many countries precisely because the armpit provides a reasonably enclosed pocket of skin-close air, though it tends to read slightly lower than oral or rectal measurements.

meanings: used in 螞螂|蚂螂[ma1 lang2]
used in 蜣螂[qiang1 lang2] and 虼螂[ge4 lang2]

components.note: 虫 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to an insect or small creature.
郎 (láng) is read identically to this character, "láng" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 厨房里突然出现了一只蟑螂。
example.pinyin: Chúfáng lǐ tūrán chūxiànle yī zhī zhāngláng.
example.english: A cockroach suddenly appeared in the kitchen.
example.fact: Cockroaches are famously resilient — some species can survive for weeks without food and hold their breath underwater for up to 40 minutes, adaptations that have helped them persist largely unchanged for hundreds of millions of years.

components.note: 阝 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to a hill or mound.

反 (fǎn)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "bǎn" (Mandarin "f-" often historically derives from an older "b-"/"p-" sound, with a matching rime and tone), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 大阪是日本的一座大城市。
example.pinyin: Dàbǎn shì Rìběn de yī zuò dà chéngshì.
example.english: Osaka is a major city in Japan.
example.fact: 阪 is the character used in the Japanese city name Osaka (大阪), and although the character is rare in standalone Chinese vocabulary today, it remains instantly recognizable to Chinese readers through this famous place name.

components.note: 手 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the hand.
制 (zhì) only loosely echoes "chè" — the initials are related retroflex sounds, but the rimes differ; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 他表面答应，实际上处处掣肘。
example.pinyin: Tā biǎomiàn dāyìng, shíjìshàng chùchù chèzhǒu.
example.english: On the surface he agreed, but in practice he obstructed at every turn.
example.fact: 掣肘 ('to pull someone's elbow,' meaning 'to hold someone back, to obstruct') comes from an ancient story about a ruler who deliberately jogged an official's elbow while he was writing, ruining his calligraphy to test his composure under interference.

components.note: 力 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to physical strength.
亥 (hài) only loosely echoes "hé" — sharing only the initial "h-"; the sound link is approximate rather than close.

example.hanzi: 议会投票弹劾了这位官员。
example.pinyin: Yìhuì tóupiào tánhéle zhè wèi guānyuán.
example.english: The parliament voted to impeach this official.
example.fact: 弹劾 ('to impeach') describes a formal accusation process against a public official for wrongdoing — a mechanism found in political systems worldwide, from ancient Chinese imperial censors who could formally accuse corrupt officials, to modern impeachment procedures in many countries' constitutions.

components.note: 氵 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to water.
历 (lì) is read identically to this character, "lì" — a clean phonetic match.

example.hanzi: 道路是用沥青铺成的。
example.pinyin: Dàolù shì yòng lìqīng pū chéng de.
example.english: The road is paved with asphalt.
example.fact: 沥青 (asphalt) is a byproduct of petroleum refining, and it is estimated that over 90% of paved roads in the world today use asphalt as their surface material, largely because of its durability and relatively low cost.

components.note: 米 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to rice, grain.
This element is what remains of 梁 (liáng, "bridge") when its 木 is swapped for 米; 梁's reading, liáng, matches this character's pronunciation closely.

example.hanzi: 高粱是酿造白酒的重要原料。
example.pinyin: Gāoliáng shì niàngzào báijiǔ de zhòngyào yuánliào.
example.english: Sorghum is an important raw material for brewing baijiu.
example.fact: Sorghum (高粱) is the key grain used to distill baijiu, China's most widely consumed spirit — by total volume consumed, baijiu is often cited as the best-selling liquor category in the world, even though it remains far less known internationally than whiskey or vodka.

components.note: 口 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to the mouth.
察 (chá)'s initial consonant is a close historical relative of the one in "cā" (ch- and c- are related affricate sounds, with a matching rime), and the rest of the syllable matches closely.

example.hanzi: 布料被撕开，发出嚓的一声。
example.pinyin: Bùliào bèi sī kāi, fāchū cā de yī shēng.
example.english: The fabric was torn apart with a ripping sound.
example.fact: 嚓 is a purely onomatopoeic character built from the mouth radical 口, used to represent sharp, quick sounds like tearing fabric, screeching tires, or a match striking — its meaning exists almost entirely in the sound itself rather than in any literal definition.
